stances.claim: The party-list experiment failed through three sequential institutional failures: framers left too much to Congress, Congress crafted self-contradicting textual provisions, and the SC shifted to verba legis post-Panganiban dismantling the marginalized-and-underrepresented safeguard.
Constitutional experiments should carry built-in expiry clauses of 20 years, after which they automatically end unless extended by amendment.
Federalism should not proceed before the Bangsamoro pilot is fully functioning -- applying experiment-verification-before-scaling.
Replacing one SC with four highest courts modeled on authoritarian Russia is not a solution to clogged dockets.

notable_anecdotes: CJ's self-disclosure that during his incumbency the SC liberally interpreted party-list provisions -- and after his retirement the Court turned textual and literal, scuttling the marginalized-and-underrepresented doctrine.
The rhetorical-question format itself as the column's structural device -- seven unanswered questions as civic Socratic method, inviting readers to 'conjure and circulate their own.'
The warning against importing federalism from the US, Canada, and Germany framed as the same reasoning error that produced the party-list fiasco.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban draws seven rhetorical lessons from the party-list fiasco, tracing how a nobly-conceived constitutional experiment collapsed through three sequential institutional failures: the framers left almost everything to Congress without safeguards; Congress enacted RA 7941 with textual provisions -- the 2-percent threshold, 3-seat limit -- that contradicted its own laudable aim; and the Supreme Court, after CJ Panganiban's retirement, abandoned the liberal 'marginalized and underrepresented' doctrine in favor of verba legis, allowing the rich, powerful, and dynasties to invade the party-list as a cheaper backdoor to Congress. He asks: Should constitutional experiments carry built-in expiry clauses of 20 years? Should parliamentary Germany's party-list be expected to succeed in presidential Philippines? Should federalism be imported before the Bangsamoro pilot is fully functioning? Should one SC be replaced with four courts modeled on authoritarian Russia? Should Congress have been more careful? Should it have responded to SC's calls for revision? Should the SC have continued its liberal interpretation? CJ leaves the questions unanswered, inviting readers to conjure and circulate their own.
